title: Restore justice
hook: restore our judges as at first
carry: kindness and justice, from the same throne

segments.voice: Yesterday, the great shofar and the scattered people. Your line was freedom comes first, then gathering. Today, once the people are gathered, the question of who judges them.

A landlord who ignored the law. A boss who promoted the friend. A court case that dragged on for years and ended with the side that had more money. A referee who never saw the foul. The trouble isn't just that something went wrong. It's that the place you were supposed to go when things go wrong was broken too. The eleventh blessing of the Amidah is a prayer about exactly that place.
screen: `A SYSTEM THAT DIDN'T WORK.` → `THE PLACE YOU GO, BROKEN TOO.` → `THE ELEVENTH BLESSING.`

segments.voice: It says: restore our judges as at first, and our counselors as at the beginning. Remove from us sorrow and sighing. Reign over us, You alone, with kindness and compassion, and vindicate us in judgment. Blessed are You, King who loves righteousness and justice. The first line is lifted almost word for word from Isaiah. In the old Jewish translation: "And I will restore thy judges as at the first, and thy counsellors as at the beginning." Isaiah is speaking to a Jerusalem whose leaders, he says, love bribes and ignore the orphan and the widow. The repair he imagines isn't a new system. It's a return to the old one working the way it should. Some readers hear in as at first the Torah's picture of judges: when Moses is worn out from judging everyone himself, his father-in-law Jethro tells him to find capable people who fear God, love truth and hate unjust gain. Notice what sits inside a blessing about justice: kindness and compassion. It doesn't set justice and mercy against each other. It asks for both from the same throne. It ends with two words a psalm also pairs, saying God loves them: tzedakah and mishpat, righteousness and justice. And during the ten days from Rosh Hashanah to Yom Kippur, the ending changes to the King of judgment, because tradition holds that this is the season when God judges the world.
screen: `RESTORE OUR JUDGES AS AT FIRST.` · `JETHRO: PEOPLE WHO HATE UNJUST GAIN.` · `JUSTICE WITH KINDNESS AND COMPASSION.` · `TZEDAKAH AND MISHPAT.` · then, large: `RESTORE JUSTICE.`

segments.voice: List, silently, the people who make decisions over your life, a judge, a mayor, a principal, a manager, a landlord, a referee, and pick one, picturing them on an ordinary day with a hard decision on their desk. Hold one wish for them: that they see clearly, that they can't be bought, that they're kind to the person with the least power in the room. If you pray, you can ask it.
Restore justice. Hashivah shofteinu. The Amidah's eleventh blessing: return our judges as at first, with kindness and compassion.

Your line: kindness and justice, from the same throne. A week of requests: bring us back, forgive us, see our trouble, heal us, bless the year, freedom comes first, then gathering, and now fair judges. That's day five hundred eighty-eight.

howItsDone: Hashivah shofteinu is the eleventh blessing of the weekday Amidah; during the Ten Days of Repentance its closing changes from the King who loves righteousness and justice to the King of judgment.
